topic: Development of Visual Function: Sensory Experience and Critical Periods

questions.question: What is the primary role of photoreceptors in the retina?
options: Convert light into electrical signals
Generate the optic nerve by extending axons to the thalamus
Combine information from the two eyes in binocular cortex
Produce action potentials that directly reach primary visual cortex
questions.feedback: Photoreceptors transduce light into electrical signals that are processed by retinal circuits.

questions.question: Which retinal cells generate action potentials that leave the eye through the optic nerve?
options: Bipolar cells of the inner retina
Retinal ganglion cells
Horizontal cells
Photoreceptors
questions.feedback: Retinal ganglion cells are the output neurons of the retina and their axons form the optic nerve.

questions.question: What is the main route by which retinal signals reach primary visual cortex?
options: Retina → superior colliculus → pulvinar → temporal cortex
Retina → hippocampus → V1
Retina → optic nerve → LGN → V1
Retina → spinal cord → V1
questions.feedback: Retinal ganglion cell axons reach the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, which sends thalamocortical projections to V1.

questions.question: What is a neuron's receptive field?
options: The complete set of neurotransmitters and receptors expressed by a sensory neuron during normal sensory processing
The anatomical territory occupied by the neuron's cell body
The cortical region containing neurons with similar response properties
The region of sensory space where a stimulus can modify its activity
questions.feedback: A receptive field is the region of sensory space in which stimulation can influence a neuron's activity.

questions.question: Which receptive-field organization is typical of retinal ganglion cells?
options: A concentric center-surround organization
An elongated orientation-selective organization only
A receptive field covering the entire visual field uniformly
A purely binocular receptive field requiring stimulation of both eyes
questions.feedback: Retinal ganglion cells commonly have concentric ON-center/OFF-surround or OFF-center/ON-surround receptive fields.

questions.question: What is one consequence of convergence from many photoreceptors onto fewer retinal ganglion cells?
options: Every photoreceptor retains an independent labeled line all the way to visual cortex
Each ganglion cell integrates information from a region of the retina
Retinal ganglion cells lose sensitivity to spatial differences in luminance
Signals from the two eyes are combined directly inside the retina
questions.feedback: Convergence means that a retinal ganglion cell integrates signals over a region of retinal space, defining its receptive field.

questions.question: What happens to axons from the nasal retina at the optic chiasm?
options: They remain ipsilateral and terminate in the same-side thalamic relay
They terminate directly in V1
They cross to the opposite side
They return to the retina
questions.feedback: Axons from the nasal retina cross at the optic chiasm, whereas temporal-retina axons remain ipsilateral.

questions.question: How are inputs from the two eyes organized in the LGN?
options: They are completely mixed into a single binocular layer
They are organized only according to orientation preference
They are converted into dorsal and ventral streams
They remain largely segregated into eye-specific layers
questions.feedback: In the LGN, retinal inputs from the two eyes remain largely segregated into separate layers.

questions.question: What happens to information from the two eyes in V1?
options: Cortical circuits begin to combine the previously segregated inputs
The two eyes remain completely separate throughout all cortical layers
Input from the ipsilateral eye is normally eliminated
Only the eye with higher acuity reaches visual cortex
questions.feedback: Eye-specific inputs arrive separately, but cortical circuitry in V1 begins to combine them, producing binocular neurons.

questions.question: How do many V1 receptive fields differ from retinal ganglion cell receptive fields?
options: They remain circular but become sensitive only to the overall brightness of the entire visual scene
They are elongated and selective for features such as orientation
They contain no spatial organization
They respond only to uniform illumination
questions.feedback: Many V1 neurons have elongated receptive fields and become selective for the orientation of edges or bars.

questions.question: In the classical Hubel-Wiesel feedforward model, how can orientation selectivity arise?
options: Orientation selectivity is generated when a single retinal ganglion cell expands its receptive field inside V1
LGN neurons first become orientation selective through lateral interactions, and V1 simply inherits that tuning
Aligned LGN receptive fields converge onto the same cortical neuron
The optic chiasm rotates visual images into preferred orientations
questions.feedback: The classical model proposes that spatially aligned circular LGN receptive fields converge to create an elongated cortical receptive field.

questions.question: Which function is especially associated with the dorsal visual stream?
options: Object identity and color recognition
Phototransduction in rods and cones
Segregation of retinal inputs in the LGN
Spatial processing and visually guided action
questions.feedback: The dorsal stream projects mainly toward parietal cortex and emphasizes motion, spatial position, and visually guided action.

questions.question: Which function is especially associated with the ventral visual stream?
options: Processing object form and identity
Guiding reaching movements toward spatial targets
Generating retinal waves before eye opening
Maintaining eye-specific layers in the LGN
questions.feedback: The ventral stream projects mainly toward temporal cortex and is especially involved in object form, color, and identity.

questions.question: What is visual acuity?
options: The ability to detect any change in overall brightness
The ability to resolve fine spatial detail
The ability to estimate depth using one eye
The speed at which retinal ganglion cells fire
questions.feedback: Visual acuity describes the ability to distinguish fine spatial detail, such as two nearby points.

questions.question: Why is visual acuity highest near the fovea?
options: The fovea contains the largest retinal receptive fields and therefore integrates information over wider areas
The fovea receives a direct projection to temporal cortex that bypasses the lateral geniculate nucleus
Photoreceptors are densely packed and retinal convergence is low
The optic nerve contains only foveal retinal ganglion cells
questions.feedback: Dense photoreceptor spacing and relatively low convergence preserve fine spatial sampling in the fovea.

questions.question: What does spatial frequency describe?
options: How rapidly a neuron fires action potentials
How often the eyes make saccades
How quickly a stimulus changes color over time
How rapidly luminance changes across space
questions.feedback: Spatial frequency describes the rate of luminance variation across space and is commonly expressed in cycles per degree.

questions.question: What is contrast sensitivity?
options: The ability to detect differences in luminance
The ability to identify the color of an object
The ability to resolve only the smallest possible detail
The ability to combine the two retinal images into depth
questions.feedback: Contrast sensitivity describes the ability to detect luminance differences between a stimulus and its background.

questions.question: At which spatial frequencies is human contrast sensitivity generally highest?
options: Only the very highest spatial frequencies
Intermediate spatial frequencies
Only zero spatial frequency
Equally at all spatial frequencies
questions.feedback: The contrast sensitivity function normally peaks at intermediate spatial frequencies.

questions.question: What is retinal disparity?
options: The difference in photoreceptor density between central and peripheral retina that determines how finely each region samples visual space
The difference in luminance between the center and surround of a retinal ganglion cell receptive field during local contrast processing
The difference between the images formed on the two retinas because the eyes occupy different positions
The difference in acuity between the dorsal and ventral visual streams
questions.feedback: Because the eyes view the world from slightly different positions, the two retinal images differ; this retinal disparity provides a binocular depth cue.

questions.question: Which depth cue can operate with one eye alone?
options: Retinal disparity
Binocular convergence of cortical inputs
Comparison of left- and right-retinal images
Occlusion
questions.feedback: Occlusion is a monocular cue: an object that blocks another is usually perceived as closer.

questions.question: How does linear perspective provide information about depth?
options: Parallel lines appear to converge as distance increases
Parallel lines maintain constant retinal separation as distance increases, allowing the brain to estimate depth directly
Distant objects create larger binocular disparities than nearby objects
Shadows disappear as objects move farther away
questions.feedback: In linear perspective, parallel lines appear to converge with increasing distance, providing a monocular cue to depth.

questions.question: How can shading contribute to depth perception?
options: Shading provides a direct measure of the physical distance separating the two eyes from one another
Patterns of light and shadow provide information about three-dimensional shape
Patterns of illumination determine which nasal retinal axons cross the midline at the optic chiasm
Shading is used only to detect color and not shape
questions.feedback: The distribution of light and shadow can make surfaces appear convex or concave and therefore provides information about three-dimensional form.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the visual system at birth?
options: Both anatomy and visual performance are already adult-like
The retina is mature but thalamocortical projections have not formed
Major pathways are present, but visual function is still immature
Normal vision begins only after new visual pathways are generated postnatally
questions.feedback: At birth, much of the visual pathway is anatomically organized, but acuity, contrast sensitivity, focusing, and eye-movement control remain immature.

questions.question: Approximately how does visual acuity at birth compare with adult acuity?
options: It is already equal to adult acuity
It is about twice as good as adult acuity
It is only slightly poorer and matures within days
It is about 40 times poorer
questions.feedback: Visual acuity at birth is approximately 40 times poorer than in adults.

questions.question: Which peripheral change contributes to the development of visual acuity?
options: Foveal photoreceptors become more densely packed and their outer segments elongate
The optic chiasm progressively removes ipsilateral retinal projections as spatial resolution improves during childhood
Primary visual cortex becomes less selective for fine spatial information as the retina becomes more mature
The LGN stops receiving retinal input from the two eyes
questions.feedback: Postnatal photoreceptor maturation improves retinal sampling, particularly as foveal cones become denser and their outer segments elongate.

questions.question: Which central change contributes to improving visual acuity during development?
options: V1 receptive fields become progressively larger and integrate information across broader regions of visual space
Receptive fields become smaller and cortical processing becomes more spatially precise
The retinotopic organization of the LGN becomes less precise as cortical visual processing matures
Cortical inhibition disappears as acuity improves
questions.feedback: Central maturation includes changes in LGN and V1, maturation of inhibitory circuitry, and smaller, more selective receptive fields.

questions.question: At approximately what age does high-contrast visual acuity approach adult-like values?
options: Within the first week after birth
Around 15-20 years of age
Around 5-6 years of age
Only after 30 years of age
questions.feedback: High-contrast visual acuity improves rapidly during the first year and approaches adult-like values at roughly 5-6 years, depending on the measurement.

questions.question: What happens to foveal photoreceptors during childhood?
options: They become progressively larger and farther apart, increasing convergence onto each retinal ganglion cell
They are gradually replaced by newly generated retinal ganglion cells during the first years of childhood
They migrate from the retina into the LGN
They become smaller, more densely packed, and structurally more mature
questions.feedback: During postnatal development, especially in the fovea, photoreceptors become more densely packed, elongate their outer segments, and become more regularly organized.

questions.question: What are retinal waves?
options: Spontaneous correlated activity that propagates across groups of developing retinal ganglion cells
Coordinated movements of the immature retina that mechanically stimulate photoreceptors before normal eye opening
Oscillatory activity generated only after patterned visual experience has begun to drive cortical circuits
Light waves reflected from the retina toward the lens
questions.feedback: Retinal waves are spontaneous patterns of coordinated activity that occur before normal visual experience.

questions.question: Why can retinal waves help refine developing visual connections?
options: They cause neighboring retinal neurons to fire independently, preventing local spatial correlations from forming before patterned vision
Nearby retinal neurons tend to be active together, providing spatial and temporal correlation
They replace molecular guidance by assigning every retinal ganglion cell a unique activity-defined target identity during development
They directly generate adult visual acuity by producing mature photoreceptor spacing before patterned visual experience begins
questions.feedback: Retinal waves provide structured correlations: nearby cells are more likely to be active together than widely separated cells.

questions.question: What happens when spontaneous activity in one eye is blocked with TTX during development?
options: The entire thalamus on that side disappears
The blocked retina immediately develops adult-like receptive fields
The eye-specific projection from that retina to the LGN develops abnormally and can be strongly reduced
The other eye loses its retinal ganglion cells
questions.feedback: Blocking retinal activity with TTX disrupts normal refinement and segregation of eye-specific retinogeniculate connections.

questions.question: How does contrast sensitivity change during development?
options: Sensitivity decreases as visual acuity improves
Only low spatial frequencies remain detectable in adulthood
Contrast sensitivity is adult-like at birth and changes little
Sensitivity increases and progressively higher spatial frequencies become detectable
questions.feedback: During childhood, contrast sensitivity increases and the range of efficiently processed spatial frequencies becomes broader.

questions.question: How does maturation of inhibitory circuitry contribute to visual development?
options: It helps refine cortical responses and improve selectivity for visual features
It prevents all activity-dependent changes in immature cortex
It removes center-surround organization from retinal ganglion cells
It causes retinal photoreceptors to stop responding to light
questions.feedback: Maturing inhibition helps regulate gain and sharpen visual cortical representations, contributing to improved contrast sensitivity and circuit refinement.

questions.question: What is a critical period?
options: A period when all neural plasticity is completely absent
A developmental window when particular neural circuits are especially sensitive to experience
The first hours after birth when only retinal anatomy can change
Any period of adulthood in which visual input remains constant
questions.feedback: A critical period is a developmental window during which experience can produce particularly large and persistent changes in neural circuits.

questions.question: What does the congenital cataract example show about visual development?
options: The timing of visual restoration has little effect on later visual function
Cataracts affect only the retina and never cortical development
Restoring patterned vision early generally leads to better outcomes than restoring it after prolonged deprivation
Normal visual function is guaranteed whenever the cataract is eventually removed
questions.feedback: Congenital cataract illustrates that the timing of patterned visual experience strongly influences later visual development.

questions.question: What did the case of S.B. illustrate after vision was restored in adulthood?
options: Adult surgery immediately restored normal acuity, stereopsis, and object recognition
Visual deprivation affected only color perception
Long-term deprivation had no lasting effect once the eye was repaired
Restoring optical input late did not produce normal visual perception
questions.feedback: S.B. improved after surgery but retained major deficits, showing that some visual abilities require appropriate experience during development.

questions.question: What is amblyopia?
options: Reduced visual function caused by abnormal visual experience during development
A degenerative disease caused only by retinal-cell death
A temporary reduction in acuity produced by normal adaptation to darkness
A visual deficit caused exclusively by damage to the optic nerve in adulthood
questions.feedback: Amblyopia is a developmental reduction in visual function associated with abnormal visual experience, such as cataract, strabismus, or unequal refractive error.

questions.question: What is the typical cortical effect of monocular deprivation during the critical period?
options: Both eyes gain equal cortical representation
V1 responses shift strongly toward the non-deprived eye
The deprived eye becomes more strongly represented than the open eye
All V1 neurons stop responding to either eye
questions.feedback: During the critical period, monocular deprivation shifts ocular dominance so that many cortical neurons become dominated by the open eye.

questions.question: What are ocular dominance columns?
options: Retinal layers containing only rods or only cones
LGN neurons arranged according to preferred edge orientation
Alternating cortical territories receiving stronger input from one eye or the other
Axonal bundles carrying dorsal and ventral stream information
questions.feedback: In species such as cats and primates, eye-specific geniculocortical inputs form alternating ocular-dominance territories, especially in layer IV of V1.

questions.question: What can happen after only a few days of monocular deprivation during early development?
options: No measurable cortical change occurs until deprivation lasts several months
The deprived eye immediately gains additional cortical territory
The retina permanently loses all photoreceptors
Binocular responses can decline rapidly and ocular dominance can shift toward the open eye
questions.feedback: Even brief deprivation can strongly reduce binocular responses, demonstrating the high plasticity of developing visual cortex.

questions.question: What anatomical change can follow prolonged monocular deprivation?
options: Ocular-dominance territory and geniculocortical arbors serving the deprived eye can shrink
The deprived-eye retina becomes larger than the open-eye retina
Both eyes develop identical enlarged cortical columns
The optic chiasm disappears after prolonged deprivation
questions.feedback: Prolonged monocular deprivation can transform a functional imbalance into structural reorganization, including shrinkage of deprived-eye cortical territory and axon arbors.

questions.question: Why is monocular deprivation particularly effective at changing ocular dominance?
options: Both eyes are completely inactive during deprivation
The two eyes compete under strongly unequal conditions
Monocular deprivation increases correlation between the two eyes
The open eye loses patterned visual activity
questions.feedback: During monocular deprivation, the open eye provides effective patterned activity while the deprived eye provides weak or abnormal drive, producing strong competition.

questions.question: What is the main cortical consequence of developmental strabismus?
options: Both eyes become more strongly correlated and binocular responses increase
Only the retinal photoreceptors of the deviated eye are affected
Binocular neurons are strongly reduced because corresponding inputs from the two eyes are poorly correlated
Ocular dominance becomes permanently centered on equal binocular responses
questions.feedback: Strabismus creates mismatched activity between the eyes, reducing binocular integration and impairing stereoscopic vision.

questions.question: What does synchronous versus asynchronous stimulation show about binocular development?
options: The amount of activity matters, but the timing relationship between the eyes does not
Only asynchronous activation supports binocular cortical neurons
Binocular integration develops without any dependence on neural activity
Temporal correlation between the two eyes helps determine whether their inputs become integrated
questions.feedback: Synchronous activation favors binocular convergence, whereas asynchronous activation favors more monocular organization.

questions.question: How does the effect of monocular deprivation depend on age?
options: It is largest during the critical period and smaller before or after that window
It increases steadily throughout adulthood
It is identical at every developmental age
It occurs only before retinal waves begin
questions.feedback: The same deprivation produces different effects depending on developmental age, with the strongest ocular-dominance plasticity during the critical period.

questions.question: What happens to the capacity to induce LTP in visual cortex as the critical period closes?
options: It increases without limit
It progressively decreases
It remains unchanged throughout development
It disappears before the critical period begins
questions.feedback: Closure of the critical period is accompanied by reduced LTP induction and increased stability of visual cortical synapses.

questions.question: What role does maturation of GABAergic inhibition play in critical-period plasticity?
options: Inhibition must be absent for the critical period to open
GABAergic maturation affects only the retina and not visual cortex
A sufficient level of inhibition helps establish the circuit state required for normal ocular-dominance plasticity
Increasing inhibition prevents any developmental plasticity from ever occurring
questions.feedback: Maturation of GABAergic inhibition is an important regulator of the onset and progression of critical-period plasticity.

questions.question: What is a major effect of precocious BDNF expression in developing visual cortex?
options: It prevents inhibitory circuits from maturing
It permanently increases final visual acuity beyond wild-type levels
It delays susceptibility to monocular deprivation until adulthood
It advances inhibitory maturation and shifts the critical period to earlier ages
questions.feedback: BDNF overexpression accelerates GABAergic maturation, causing visual functions and ocular-dominance plasticity to follow an earlier developmental timetable without increasing the final visual capability.

questions.question: What do perineuronal nets contribute to in mature visual cortex?
options: Circuit stabilization and reduced juvenile-like plasticity
Generation of retinal waves before vision begins
Formation of photoreceptor outer segments in the fovea
Crossing of nasal retinal axons at the optic chiasm
questions.feedback: Perineuronal nets accumulate around subsets of neurons during maturation and are associated with greater circuit stability and reduced juvenile-like plasticity.

questions.question: What happens when perineuronal nets are degraded with chondroitinase ABC in adult visual cortex?
options: All cortical responses to visual stimulation are permanently abolished
Ocular-dominance plasticity can reappear in response to monocular deprivation
Adult visual cortex becomes unable to respond to either eye
Photoreceptor density in the fovea immediately increases
questions.feedback: Degrading mature extracellular-matrix constraints with chondroitinase ABC can restore a more juvenile-like capacity for ocular-dominance plasticity.
